- **Drink with attention.** The question the ayat put to us is the one quoted from Sūrat Al-Wāqiʿah: *"why then do you not give thanks?"* Water is the blessing used most and noticed least. Ibn Kathir's counterfactual is the cure — it could have been salty and undrinkable.
- **You are not the one taking care of it.** That is Ibn Kathir's phrase. Effort is asked of you; the springs, the wells and the rivers are maintained by Someone else. And the same passage that says you cannot store the water says He is the Inheritor of the earth and everyone on it.
- **Read the shortfall correctly.** On the narration Ibn Kathir cites, rain is divided between the years and the lands as He wills — it rains here a year and there a year. Where the rain does not come, the sources point you to His dividing and His wisdom, not to a failure in the arrangement.
- **Move to the front.** On the reading of Hasan al-Basri, al-Qurtubi and others, being *mustaqdim* is something you decide several times a day: coming early to the prayer, taking the first row, stepping forward for what is good. And on Ka'b's practice, if you end up at the back, be there hoping in the barakah of a better servant ahead of you — never in complacency.
- **Take the gathering personally.** Ayah 24 does not speak about generations at a distance. Its wording is "the first generations **of you**." You are already known, already counted among those He will gather.

passages.title: Man from clay, jinn from fire, Iblis refuses
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat tell the story of where we came from — and of the first act of arrogance in creation. Allah names the raw material of man and the raw material of the jinn (26–27), then rewinds to the moment before Adam existed, when Allah announced him to the angels, breathed into him of His spirit, and commanded them to fall in prostration (28–29). Every angel obeyed (30). One creature present among them refused (31). What holds the passage together is a single thread: the substance a creature is made of decides nothing — the honour lies in what Allah put into man and in obedience to what Allah commands.

## Two creations, two substances (26–27)

**"Sounding clay from moulded black mud."** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah that *salsal* means dry mud — clay that has dried out so far that it rings or rattles when struck. He anchors this by comparing the Qur'an with the Qur'an, quoting *"He created man from sounding clay like the potter's clay, and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire"* (55:14–15). A second report from Mujahid glosses *salsal* as "putrid," but Ibn Kathir sets that aside with a principle worth learning by itself: **it is more appropriate to interpret an ayah with another ayah** than with anything else.

The second phrase, *ḥamaʾ masnūn*, Ibn Kathir explains as the dried clay that comes from mud, which is soil; "altered" here, he says, means **smooth**. So the picture is not of something repulsive but of earth worked and refined — mud smoothed and then dried hard enough to ring.

**The jinn came first.** In ayah 27, *"And the jinn, We created earlier"* means, in Ibn Kathir's words, **before creating humans**. Their substance is *nār al-samūm*. Ibn 'Abbas said it is "the smokeless flame that kills." Ibn Kathir then relays a report — Abu Dawud at-Tayalisi, from Shu'bah, from Abu Ishaq, who visited 'Umar al-Asamm during an illness and was told by him of something he had heard from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud: that this *samūm* is **one of the seventy parts** of the smokeless fire from which the jinn were created; the narration then follows with the recitation of this very ayah. And Ibn Kathir cites a hadith he identifies as being "in the Sahih": *the angels were created from light, the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire, and Adam was created from that which has been described to you.* Three orders of creation, three substances — light, fire, clay.

**Why mention clay at all?** Because a modern ear hears "clay" as a put-down. Ibn Kathir hears the opposite. He states plainly that this ayah **is intended to point out the noble nature, good essence and pure origin of Adam**. Allah is not apologising for the material; He is presenting it — and presenting it as honour.

## Adam announced before he existed (28)

Ayah 28 shifts the camera backwards: *"And when your Lord said to the angels: I am going to create a man from sounding clay of altered mud."* Ibn Kathir sums up what is happening here: **Allah informs us of how He mentioned Adam to His angels before He created him, and how He honoured him by commanding the angels to prostrate to him.**

Notice the sequence. Adam is spoken about before he is made. His description is published to the highest creation before a single limb of him exists. And the description Allah gives is exactly the one from ayah 26 — the sounding clay, the smoothed mud. Allah does not hide the humble ingredient; He announces it, and in the same breath announces the honour that will follow it.

## "And I breathed into him of My spirit" (29)

Ayah 29 sets the trigger for the prostration: *"So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down before him, prostrating."* The order matters. The angels are not told to bow to a clay figure. They are told to bow **once the fashioning is complete and the spirit has been breathed in**. The clay alone commands nothing; the clay carrying what Allah placed in it commands everything.

**"Of My spirit" is a phrase of honour.** Ibn Kathir glosses *of My spirit* as *the soul which I created for him* — that is, the *rūḥ* is itself created, brought into being by Allah like everything else, so attaching it to Himself confers dignity on it rather than dividing off some piece of His own being. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point from the other side: Allah attributed the spirit to Himself **so that the superior status of the human spirit out of the entire creation becomes evident** — because it came into existence with no material substance, purely under the Divine command, and because it has a unique ability to accept and absorb the manifestations of Divine light, an ability that exists in the spirit of no other living creature.

**What is the spirit? An honest answer.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens this question with unusual candour. Is the *rūḥ* a physical entity or pure essence? Scholars have disagreed for a long time; Ash-Shaykh 'Abd al-Rauf al-Munawi records **up to a thousand positions** taken on it — and Maʿārif's own verdict is that they are all based on conjecture and **none of them can be called certain**. Imam al-Ghazali, Imam Razi and the mystic scholars and thinkers held that it is not a physical entity but pure essence, Razi advancing twelve arguments for it. The **majority of the 'Ulama' of the Muslim Ummah**, however, declare the *rūḥ* to be a highly refined physical entity.

The word *nafkh* means to blow, to breathe into. Maʿārif (citing *Bayan al-Qur'an*) shows that either view makes sense of it: if the spirit is a refined physical entity, "breathing in" is evident by itself; if it is pure essence, "breathing in" means **establishing its connection to the body**. This is a place to hold the text firmly and the theory loosely.

**Tafsir Mazhari's model.** Rather than wade through the thousand positions, Maʿārif refers the reader to a special study by Qadi Thana'ullah Panipati in *Tafsir Mazhari*. He distinguishes two kinds of spirit:

- **The higher (*ʿulwī*) spirit** — bereft of matter, a creation of Allah whose reality is difficult to comprehend. The masters of insight by illumination (*ahl al-kashf*) see its real station as above the Throne, because it is more refined than the Throne. It is sensed in five degrees: *qalb* (heart), *rūḥ* (spirit), *sirr* (mystery), *khafī* (secret) and *akhfā* (most secret) — all belonging to the refinements of the domain of the Divine command, to which the Qur'an hints in *"Say: the spirit is from the command of my Lord"* (17:85).
- **The lower (*siflī*) spirit** — a refined vapour that emerges from the combination of the four elements of the body: fire, water, dust and air. This lower spirit is what is called the *nafs*, the self.

Allah made the lower spirit a **mirror** of the higher. Panipati's image: hold a mirror to the sun and, though the sun is far, far away, its reflection lands in the glass — the mirror begins to glow like the sun and even receives heat enough to burn a piece of cloth. So too the higher spirits: for all their purity and detachment and distance, their reflection appears in the mirror of the lower spirit and transfers their states and effects into it.

That lower spirit, now armed with what it has acquired from above, **first gets connected with the heart muscle of the body — and that connection is itself another name for life**. From the heart it infuses life and the cognitions it has received, then circulates through the thin veins spread throughout the body until it reaches every part of it. This infusion, Panipati says, is what is called the "blowing or breathing of the spirit," because it bears close resemblance to blowing into something.

**Ten elements, not one.** Maʿārif draws the conclusion. Dust is the dominant element in man's creation — which is why his creation is attributed to clay — but in reality man is a combination of **ten** elements: five from the universe of creation (*ʿālam al-khalq*): fire, water, dust, air, and the refined vapour from these four which is the lower spirit or *nafs*; and five from the universe of the Divine command (*ʿālam al-amr*): *qalb*, *rūḥ*, *sirr*, *khafī* and *akhfā*.

It is because of this **comprehensive making** of the human model that man became deserving of Divine vice-regency — very much capable of absorbing the light that helps him know his Lord, and of sustaining a lifelong burning quest on the path of love and longing for Him, whose outcome, though unspecified as to its actual state, is communion with the Divine. Maʿārif supports this with the words of the Prophet ﷺ that **one shall be with whoever one loves**. And since human beings have this ability to absorb the manifestations of Divine light, and have been given this honour, it came to be the dictate of Divine wisdom that man be made the object of prostration by the angels: *"fall down before him, prostrating"* (29).

## Every single one of them (30)

Ayah 30 is the answer to the command: *"So the angels prostrated themselves, all of them together."* The wording piles emphasis on emphasis — *kulluhum ajmaʿūn*, "all of them, together." What ayah 29 commanded, ayah 30 records as done.

And notice what their prostration was for. Ibn Kathir keeps the honour exactly where the ayah puts it: Allah **honoured Adam by commanding the angels to prostrate to him**. Maʿārif says the same from the side of wisdom — because of what Allah had placed in man, it became the dictate of Divine wisdom that he be made the object of the angels' prostration. The angels did not weigh Adam up and decide he was worth bowing to; Allah commanded, and they went down.

## "Except Iblis" (31)

Then one exception, and the whole passage turns on it: *"except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrated."*

**Was Iblis even commanded?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question, since ayat 28–30 present the command as addressed to the angels. The answer is decisive: in Surah al-A'raf, Allah says to him, *"What stopped you from prostrating when I ordered you?"* (7:12) — which shows the command was given to Iblis as well. Maʿārif explains the mechanism: the order was originally given to the angels, and Iblis, being present among them, was covered by it **as a corollary** — when the command went forth for the most august creation of Allah, the angels, to pay homage to Adam, it was obvious that any other creation was bound to follow suit. And Maʿārif notes the telling detail: for this very reason, **Iblis never answered that he had not been asked to prostrate in the first place** and so could not be charged with non-compliance.

**The wording carries the charge.** Maʿārif finds a hint in the exact phrasing. Allah did not say *abā an yasjuda* — "he refused to prostrate." He said *abā an yakūna maʿa as-sājidīn* — **"he refused to be among those who prostrated."** This indicates that the main prostrators were, after all, the angels, and that Iblis, being present with them, was reason-bound to join them. So the Divine wrath, Maʿārif says, was against **his failure to join**. His sin was not merely a missing action; it was standing apart from a body that was bowing.

**What was underneath the refusal.** Ibn Kathir names it without softening: his enemy Iblis, amidst all the angels, refused to prostrate to Adam **out of envy, disbelief, stubbornness, arrogance and false pride**. And Ibn Kathir sets that refusal beside Iblis's own words elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"I am better than him; You created me from fire and him You created from clay"* (7:12), and *"Do you see this one whom You have honoured above me?"* (17:62).

There is the whole disease in one sentence. Iblis weighs substance against substance — my fire against his clay — and concludes he is worth more. He never mentions the spirit at all, which was the one thing the command was actually built on. Allah had described that clay, in Ibn Kathir's reading, precisely to point out **noble nature, good essence and pure origin**. Iblis looked at the same material and saw only something beneath him.

## Living it

**Arrogance is a way of seeing, not just a way of behaving.** Iblis's error was a comparison: my raw material against his. Every version of that comparison since — lineage, race, wealth, learning, seniority — repeats the reasoning of the first refuser. And it is worth remembering, when the comparison tempts us, that Allah described that same clay in terms of honour.

**Notice the shape of the sin: refusing to be *among* those who prostrate.** Iblis was there among the angels. The command went forth in his hearing. He simply held himself apart from the ranks that went down, and it was that failure to join, Maʿārif says, that the Divine wrath fell upon. There is a particular danger in being present at obedience while standing outside it — attending without joining, watching the sujud of others as a spectator.

**Nothing about him lacked information.** He was addressed by Allah — *"What stopped you from prostrating when I ordered you?"* — and he answered back in his own words. Ibn Kathir's list is a diagnosis worth keeping: envy, disbelief, stubbornness, arrogance and false pride can sit alongside knowing exactly what has been commanded and by whom. Knowledge alone did not save him; only prostration would have.

**And take the honour seriously.** The angels were commanded to bow to a creature made of dried mud because Allah had fashioned him and breathed into him of a spirit He attributed to Himself. That capacity — to absorb the light by which a person knows his Lord — is, as Maʿārif puts it, why man became deserving of vice-regency. It is a dignity given for use, and the words of the Prophet ﷺ are the measure of where that use ends: **one shall be with whoever one loves.**

passages.title: Iblis questioned, expelled, and granted respite
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Ayat 32–38 unfold like a trial. One creature has refused a command; he is called by name, asked for his reason, sentenced — and then, astonishingly, granted the one thing he asks for.

What holds these seven ayat together is that they are a single unbroken dialogue, with no narration in between: Allah speaks (32), Iblis answers (33), Allah passes sentence (34–35), Iblis petitions (36), Allah answers the petition (37–38). Everything we learn here, we learn from what is said.

## The moment we are dropped into

Ibn Kathir sets the scene from the ayat just before. Allah told the angels He was going to create a man from dried, sounding clay of altered mud (ayah 28); when He had fashioned him completely and breathed into him of His spirit, they were to fall down prostrating before him (ayah 29). The angels prostrated, "all of them together" (ayah 30) — except Iblis, who "refused to be among the prostrate" (ayah 31).

Ibn Kathir draws out what the command itself means before anyone disobeys it: Allah "mentioned Adam to His angels before He created him," and He "honored him by commanding the angels to prostrate to him." So the prostration was an act of obedience to Allah and an honour placed on Adam. Iblis, says Ibn Kathir, was "amidst all the angels" and refused "out of envy, disbelief, stubbornness, arrogance, and false pride" — five diseases, named plainly, and worth sitting with one at a time.

## Ayah 32: "What is the matter with you?"

He is called by name — *yā Iblīs* — and asked a question: *mā laka allā takūna maʿa al-sājidīn*, "What is your reason for not being among the prostrate?" (Ibn Kathir's rendering). Notice the order of the passage: the question comes first, his answer second (ayah 33), and the sentence only after that (ayah 34). He is asked for his reason before anything is pronounced over him, and the words the sentence follows are his own.

Notice too the shape of the question. It is not "why did you not prostrate?" but "what is the matter with you that you are **not among those prostrating**?" That phrasing is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds something important.

## Was Iblis even commanded? — the question Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers

Read ayat 29–31 on their own and the command looks as though it was addressed only to the angels. Yet in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf, Allah says to Iblis directly: *mā manaʿaka allā tasjuda idh amartuka* — "What stopped you from prostrating **when I ordered you**?" (7:12). So was the order given to him or not?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān resolves it like this. The command was originally given to the angels; but Iblis was present among them, and so he too was covered by it as a corollary. The reasoning runs from the greater to the lesser: when the command went forth to the most august creation of Allah — the angels — that they pay their homage to Sayyidnā Ādam (peace be upon him), it was obvious that any other creation was bound to follow suit. A lesser creature cannot claim exemption from a homage required of the greatest.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then adds a supporting observation from the scene itself: **Iblis never made the opposite argument.** He never responded by saying that he had not been asked to prostrate in the first place and so could not be charged with non-compliance. The defence was available and he did not use it — which fits exactly with his having been under the command.

And perhaps, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — the word is its own, offered as a possibility rather than a certainty — the Qur'an's wording contains a hint in that direction. Allah did not say Iblis *abā an yasjuda*, "he refused to prostrate." He said *abā an yakūna maʿa al-sājidīn*, "he refused to be among those who prostrated" (ayah 31), and the question in ayah 32 keeps that same construction. The main prostrators were, after all, the angels; Iblis, being present with them, was reason-bound to join them. The divine wrath, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, was against his failure **to join**.

That distinction is worth carrying home. The question put to Iblis was not why he failed to prostrate, but why he was not among those who did.

## Ayah 33: the answer

*Lam akun li-asjuda li-basharin* — "I am not one to prostrate myself to a human, whom You created from dried (sounding) clay of altered mud."

The description he reaches for is not new: "dried (sounding) clay of altered mud" is the very phrase Allah had used in ayah 28 when announcing that He would create this man. In Allah's mouth it was an announcement of what He was about to make; in the reply of Iblis it becomes the ground of a comparison.

Ibn Kathir places this statement alongside two others of Iblis in the Qur'an — "this is like when he said":

- *"I am better than him (Adam), You created me from Fire and him You created from clay"* (7:12).
- *"Do you see this one whom You have honoured above me…"* (17:62).

Read the three together with Ibn Kathir's five words in hand — envy, disbelief, stubbornness, arrogance, false pride — and notice what is on that list and what is not. There is no appetite on it, and no bodily weakness. Every item is a condition of the heart.

## Ayat 34–35: expelled, and cursed until the Day of Recompense

*Fa-akhruj minhā fa-innaka rajīm* — "Then leave, for verily, you are an outcast" (Ibn Kathir's rendering).

Ibn Kathir describes this as an **unconditional** command to leave: nothing in it is offered as negotiable. What is the "it" he must leave? The Arabic gives only a pronoun, *minhā*, "from it." The translation before you supplies "Paradise"; Ibn Kathir explains it as **the position he held among the highest of heights**. Either way the substance of the sentence is the same: the place he would not stand among the prostrators in is the place he is now put out of.

*Rajīm*, rendered "outcast," Ibn Kathir glosses simply as **cursed**. Ayah 35 makes that lasting: "the curse shall be upon you until the Day of Recompense." Ibn Kathir's own image is of a curse that **hounds** him until the Day of Resurrection — not a verdict pronounced once and left behind, but something that stays with him for the whole length of his reprieve.

**A report about the curse.** Ibn Kathir writes: "It was reported that Saʿīd bin Jubayr said: 'When Allah cursed Iblis, his image into something different from that of the angels, and he made a sound like a bell. Every bell that rings on this earth until the Day of Resurrection is part of that.'" Ibn Kathir adds that this was reported by Ibn Abi Hatim. Three things are worth being clear about. First, the wording of the report as it stands in the text before us is defective — a word appears to have dropped out of the opening clause — and it is given here as it stands rather than quietly repaired. Second, this is the saying of an early authority, not a statement of the Prophet ﷺ. Third, Ibn Kathir himself introduces it with "it was reported." Take it as the commentators pass it on, not as something to build doctrine upon.

## Ayat 36–38: what he asked for, and what he was given

*Rabbi fa-anẓirnī ilā yawmi yubʿathūn* — "O my Lord! Then give me respite until the Day they (the dead) will be resurrected."

He still addresses Allah as *Rabbi*, "my Lord." He speaks of a day when the dead will be raised. And what he asks for, in the words the ayah records, is time.

Ayah 37 answers using a word from the very root he used. He said *anẓirnī*, "give me respite"; the answer is *fa-innaka min al-munẓarīn*, "then verily, you are of those reprieved." What he has is not something he seized. It is a reprieve, granted — and ayah 38 sets its end: *ilā yawmi al-waqti al-maʿlūm*, "until the Day of the time appointed."

There is a small shift in wording worth noticing. Iblis asked for "the Day they will be resurrected"; the answer names "the Day of the time appointed." Ibn Kathir heads this whole section "The Expulsion of Iblis from Jannah, and **His Reprieve until the Day of Resurrection**" — so he reads the appointed time as that Day. The reprieve is real, and it is dated.

## Living it

**The command that reaches the room reaches you.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's whole argument is that Iblis could not stand behind "I was not the one addressed" — and never even tried to. When obedience is going on around you, the question that was put to him is worth putting to yourself: not whether your name was called out, but why you were not among them.

**Look again at the five.** Envy, disbelief, stubbornness, arrogance, false pride. Ibn Kathir's list describes a heart, not a hunger. A person can guard himself carefully against the sins of the body and still be carrying something from that list.

**Do not weigh people by their material.** The reply in ayah 33 measures a human being by what he was made from; 7:12 states the comparison outright — fire against clay. Ibn Kathir, meanwhile, describes the command as an honour Allah placed on Adam. The two ways of reckoning a person's worth are set side by side in this passage, and one of them is answered with expulsion.

**Rank does not protect you.** On Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 34, the position Iblis was expelled from was among the highest of heights, and he had held it amidst the angels. Long standing in high company did not survive one refusal.

**And there is a limit set on your enemy.** Ibn Kathir calls him exactly that — "His enemy Iblis." What ayat 37–38 tell you about that enemy is that his time is a granted reprieve, and it has an appointed end.

passages.title: Satan's vow to tempt, and Hell's seven gates
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat close the conversation between Allah and Iblis that began with his refusal to prostrate to Sayyidnā Adam (peace be upon him). Iblis states his life's programme — he will adorn the path of error for the children of Adam on the earth and mislead them all — and Allah answers him with a verdict: a road that leads back to Him, a boundary Iblis cannot cross, and a promised destination with seven gates. What holds the passage together is that it is a dialogue: two claims and two replies, ending not in argument but in judgement.

## How Iblis came to be standing there

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a detail earlier in the sūrah. The command was addressed to the angels, yet in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf Allah says to Iblis, "What stopped you from prostrating when I ordered you?" (7:12) — so the command bound him too. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the command was originally given to the angels, but Iblis was present among them and so was covered by it as a corollary: when the command went forth to the most august of Allah's creation that they honour Adam, any other creation was bound to follow suit. This is why Iblis never offered the obvious defence — that he had never been asked to prostrate in the first place, and so could not be charged with disobeying. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees a possible hint of this in the Qurʼān's wording: rather than "he refused to prostrate," what was said was **"he refused to be among those who prostrated."** The main prostraters were the angels; Iblis, standing with them, was reason-bound to join them. So, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the Divine wrath was against his failure to join.

## "My Lord — because You misled me"

Notice how ayah 39 opens. He addresses Allah as **Rabbi** — *my Lord* — and in the same breath lays his fall at His door. Ibn Kathir introduces the whole speech as an account of "the rebellion and arrogance of Iblis": the excuse itself is the crime continuing.

The key phrase is **bimā aghwaytanī**, which Ibn Kathir glosses simply, "because You misled me and misguided me." And the same word family comes back through the passage, three times in these few ayat. Following it is the fastest way to feel the shape of the argument:

- **أَغْوَيْتَنِي** (39) — "Because You misled me," says Iblis, of himself.
- **وَلَأُغْوِيَنَّهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ** (39) — "and I shall mislead them all," which Ibn Kathir glosses: "just as You have misled me and have ordained that for me."
- **مِنَ الْغَاوِينَ** (42) — in Allah's reply: "except those of the astray who follow you."

So Iblis wants his own ruin to be someone else's doing, and everyone else's ruin to be his own doing. Look at how ayah 42 answers that second half. The only people the verse places within his reach are those it calls "the astray who follow you" — they are described as *following* him, and Ibn Kathir explains the first part of the verse as, "you will have no way to reach those for whom I have decreed guidance." That is the whole extent of his reach, and the passage states it in Allah's own voice.

## The one thing he vows to do

**"La-uzayyinanna lahum"** — Ibn Kathir renders it, "I shall indeed adorn the path of error for them," and tells us who "them" refers to: "for the progeny of Adam."

Then comes **fī al-arḍ**, "on the earth," and Ibn Kathir spells out what the adorning involves in practice: "I will make sin dear to them, and will encourage, provoke and harass them to commit sin."

The order in Ibn Kathir's own explanation is worth pausing on. Making sin *dear* comes first; the encouraging, provoking and harassing follow after. The work begins at the level of a person's affections, before it ever reaches his limbs.

## The exception he cannot help admitting

Ayah 40 is remarkable because it comes from Iblis's own mouth: **"except Your chosen servants among them"** — إِلَّا عِبَادَكَ مِنْهُمُ الْمُخْلَصِينَ. Ibn Kathir renders it "Except Your chosen, (guided) servants among them," and places it alongside Iblis's boast in Sūrah al-Isrāʼ: "Do you see this one whom You have honoured above me, if You give me respite until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize and mislead his offspring, all but a few!" (17:62). Note what that companion verse assumes: the honour belongs to Allah's giving — *whom **You** have honoured* — and Iblis, even while resenting it, concedes the point.

Even in his most defiant moment, then, the enemy admits there is a category he cannot touch. Read the passage in order and this is a mercy: the boundary of Iblis's power is announced in his own vow, in ayah 40, before Allah confirms it in ayah 42.

## Allah's reply: a road, and a watcher

**"Hādhā ṣirāṭun ʿalayya mustaqīm"** (ayah 41). Ibn Kathir tells us the tone first: this is Allah "threatening and warning Iblis." The renderings before us bring out its range — the translation gives "This is the Way, binding on Me," and Ibn Kathir gives "This is the way which will lead straight to Me."

Ibn Kathir explains the sense as: *all of you will return to Me, and I will reward or punish you according to your deeds — if they are good then I will reward you, and if they are bad then I will punish you.* He supports it with two ayat: "Verily, your Lord is ever watchful" (89:14), and "And it is up to Allah to show the right way" (16:9).

So Iblis has just declared he will lay a crooked path across the earth, and the answer is a straight road on which every traveller arrives back at Allah and is requited for what he did. Iblis can decorate a detour; he cannot change where the road ends.

## "You shall have no authority over My servants"

The word in ayah 42 is **sulṭān**, rendered "authority" in the translation before us and "power" in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering — "My servants are such that you have no power over them." Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: "you will have no way to reach those for whom I have decreed guidance."

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question an honest reader will already be asking. From this verse we learn that there are special, chosen servants of Allah who are not affected by Shayṭān's deception. But within this very story it has also been said that his deception worked in the case of Sayyidnā Adam and Ḥawwāʼ (peace be upon them). And about the noble Companions the Qurʼān says: "Shaitan had but made them slip for some of their deeds" (3:155) — which tells us that there was an occasion, during the Battle of Uḥud, when the enemy's plan worked against them as well.

The answer Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives is precise, and it is worth holding on to. The immunity being described is **not** that such servants never slip. It is that their hearts and minds never come under Shayṭān's power and sway to the extent that they would not become alerted to their error at all — and so be deprived of the repentance they need for ever — nor that they fall into some sin whose forgiveness becomes impossible.

And the two episodes offer no contradiction, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, precisely because of how they ended: Adam and Ḥawwāʼ made their *tawbah* and that repentance was accepted; the noble Companions likewise made their *tawbah*, and whatever sin they had fallen into through Shayṭān's scheming was forgiven.

That is a doctrine of protection that fits real life. The mark of Allah's servant is not a spotless record; it is that the alarm still rings, and he still turns back.

## The enemy's own confession

For this ayah Ibn Kathir relays a report that Ibn Jarir mentioned from Yazid bin Qusayt. It concerns a prophet who is not named. The prophets, he said, used to have places of worship outside their cities; when a prophet wanted to consult his Lord about something he would go out to his place of worship, pray as Allah decreed, and then ask Him about whatever was concerning him.

Once, while such a prophet was at his place of worship, the enemy of Allah — Iblis — came and sat between him and the qiblah. The prophet said, "I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan." The enemy of Allah said, "Do you know who you are seeking refuge from? Here he is!" The prophet said it again — and he repeated that three times.

Then the enemy of Allah proposed a trade: "Tell me about anything in which you will be saved from me." The prophet twice said, "No, you tell me about something in which you can overpower the son of Adam?" Each of them was insisting that the other answer first. Then the prophet said, Allah says: **"Certainly, you shall have no authority over My servants, except those of the astray who follow you."** The enemy of Allah said, "I heard this before you were even born." The prophet went on: "And Allah says, *And if an evil whisper comes to you from Shaytan then seek refuge with Allah. Verily, He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing* (7:200). By Allah, I never sense that you are near but I seek refuge with Allah from you."

At that the enemy of Allah said: "You have spoken the truth. In this way you will be saved from me." Then the prophet said, "Tell me in what ways you overpower the son of Adam." He said:

> "I seize him at times of anger and times of desire."

Two doors, named by the one who uses them. When you are angry and when you are wanting, you are standing in the draught. That is precisely the moment the prophet's words — "I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan" — stop being a formula and become a rescue.

## The promised place, and its seven gates

Ayah 43 answers Iblis's promise with Allah's. He had said *I will adorn, I will mislead*; Allah says Hell is **their destined place, all together** — or, in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "the place promised for them all." Ibn Kathir explains: "Hell is the abode designated for all those who follow Iblis," citing "but those of the sects that reject it (the Qurʼān), the Fire will be their promised meeting place" (11:17). Every promise Iblis makes in ayah 39 is kept only in this sense: he does deliver his followers somewhere, and this is where.

Then ayah 44: **"It has seven gates, to each a group of them is designated."** On what the seven gates are, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a genuine difference among the scholars:

- According to a narration of Sayyidnā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), reported by Imām Aḥmad, Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī and al-Bayhaqī, the seven gates are **seven levels, one upon the other**.
- Some others have taken these as common gates, every gate **reserved for a special kind of sinner** (Qurṭubī).

On **"li-kulli bābin minhum juzʼun maqsūm"** — "for each of those gates is a class assigned" — Ibn Kathir explains that for each gate a portion of the followers of Iblis have been decreed, "and they will have no choice in the matter. May Allah save us from that." Yet the apportioning is not arbitrary: "Each one will enter a gate according to his deeds, and will settle in a level of Hell according to his deeds."

For this Ibn Kathir cites a report: Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Samurah bin Jundub reported from the Prophet ﷺ, concerning "for each of those gates is a class assigned," that he said: **"Among the people of Hell are those whom the Fire will swallow up to the ankles, and those whom it will swallow up to the waist, and those whom it will swallow up to the collarbone."** The degree, Ibn Kathir adds, depends upon their deeds.

That is a sobering picture, but note what it establishes: even in the Fire, exact justice. Every portion is measured against what a person actually did.

## What the passage asks of you

- **Recognise the method.** He adorns. Ibn Kathir's description of ayah 39 begins with making sin *dear* — the encouraging, provoking and harassing come after. If something forbidden has started to look beautiful, reasonable, overdue, that is the work being described, and it is happening at the level of your affections first.
- **Watch the two doors.** Anger and desire, named by the enemy himself in the report above. Slow down at exactly those two moments.
- **Use the refuge, not the argument.** In that account, when the prophet quoted ayah 42, Iblis brushed it aside: "I heard this before you were even born." But when the prophet added the command to seek refuge (7:200) and said, "By Allah, I never sense that you are near but I seek refuge with Allah from you," the enemy conceded outright: "You have spoken the truth. In this way you will be saved from me." The method he could not answer was turning to Allah, every single time.
- **Do not read ayah 42 as a licence, or your slips as a verdict.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading is the balance: the protected are not the sinless; they are the ones never left unalerted to their error and so never left without repentance. Adam and Ḥawwāʼ repented and were accepted; the Companions repented and were forgiven. The door Iblis can never shut is the door of *tawbah*.
- **Remember where both roads end.** Ayah 41: all of us return to Allah, and He requites according to deeds. Iblis can make the detour look lovely. He cannot change the destination.

passages.title: Gardens for the righteous; mercy and torment announced
passages.tafsir:
**These six ayat are the second half of a pair.** Ibn Kathir gives us the hinge in one sentence: "Since Allah mentioned the condition of the people of Hell, He followed that by mentioning the people of Paradise." Having shown us those who rejected, Allah now turns to the people of Taqwa — and the passage moves in a single unbroken arc: the place they arrive at (45), the words spoken at the gate (46), the bitterness lifted out of their hearts (47), the guarantee that none of it will fade or be taken back (48), and finally, in ayat 49–50, the announcement the Prophet ﷺ is ordered to carry to Allah's servants: *I am truly the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. And My torment is indeed the most painful torment.*

That last pair is what holds the unit together. Everything described in 45–48 is mercy; ayah 50 keeps the reader from ever taking that mercy for granted.

*A note on one word you will meet several times below.* Ibn Kathir repeatedly points to "the report in the Sahih" or "the Sahihs." *Sahih* is the standard term for a hadith that has been rigorously authenticated, and by extension for the collections that gather such hadith. When Ibn Kathir says a report is "in the Sahih," he is telling us it carries that grade. He does not name which collection — so neither will we.

## Ayah 45 — Gardens and springs

"Indeed, the righteous will be amid Gardens and springs."

Ibn Kathir renders the same phrase as "Truly, those who have Taqwa, will dwell in Gardens and water springs" — keeping the Arabic word *Taqwa* rather than replacing it with an English equivalent. Set the two renderings side by side and you have the sense the commentators are working with: these are the people whose relationship with Allah shapes how they live.

Ibn Kathir keeps his comment on this ayah deliberately plain: "He tells us that they will dwell in Gardens and water springs." Gardens and flowing springs — the setting is established first, and everything the rest of the passage describes happens inside it.

## Ayah 46 — "Enter in peace and security"

"˹It will be said to them,˺ 'Enter in peace and security.'"

The words in brackets are supplied by the translator, and Ibn Kathir's own rendering supplies them too: "(It will be said to them): 'Enter it in peace and security.'" Both read this as speech addressed to the arriving guests — a welcome spoken at the threshold.

Ibn Kathir unpacks the two words of that welcome:

- **"in peace"** — "meaning free of all problems."
- **"in security"** — "meaning free from all fear and concern. They will not have any fear of expulsion, nor will they fear that their condition will be disrupted or end."

Notice what that second gloss quietly identifies. The thing that spoils every good state in this world is often not the state itself but the anxiety attached to it: that it will be taken, that it will change, that we will be put out. Ibn Kathir says that anxiety is cut away at the door. And ayah 48 will come back to exactly that promise and make it explicit.

## Ayah 47 — The one thing they are not allowed to bring in with them

This is the richest ayah of the passage, and the commentators spend most of their attention here.

"And We shall remove any deep feeling of bitterness from their breasts. (So they will be like) brothers facing each other on thrones."

**The word is *ghill*.** Ibn Kathir's translator renders it "any deep feeling of bitterness"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it grudge and malice. It is the residue left in a chest after a quarrel — the thing that survives long after the argument is over.

**The removal is complete.** Abu Umamah is reported to have said: "The people of Paradise will enter Paradise with whatever enmity is left in their hearts from this world. Then, when they come together, Allah will remove whatever hatred the world has left in their hearts." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same in its own words — the grudges "will be totally washed away." Not some of them, not the worst of them.

Ibn Kathir is scrupulous about the Abu Umamah report. He tells us plainly that "Al-Qasim bin ʿAbdur-Rahman is weak in his reports from Abu Umamah," and only then adds that the meaning is nonetheless "in accord with the report in the Sahih." That is worth pausing on as a piece of method: the commentator names the weakness in his own evidence before telling you why he still thinks the meaning stands.

**Ibn ʿAbbas's picture of how it happens.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from Sayyidna ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas that when the people of Jannah enter, two streams of water are first presented to them. They drink from the first, and every mutual grudge carried over from the world — grudges whose effects naturally survived right through to the end — is totally washed away, and in its place they feel love for one another in their hearts. The reasoning given is worth sitting with: *mutual bickering is itself virtually a pain and punishment, and Jannah is free of all pain.* Resentment is not merely unattractive; it is suffering. A Paradise that still contained it would not be Paradise.

**The bridge before the gate.** Ibn Kathir cites what he identifies as a report in the Sahih, where Qatadah says that Abu al-Mutawakkil an-Naji told them that Abu Saʿid al-Khudri reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "The believers will be removed from the Fire, and they will be detained on a bridge between Paradise and Hell. Then judgment will be passed between them concerning any wrong they have committed in this world against one another, until they are cleansed and purified. Then permission will be given to them to enter Paradise."

So the ayah is not describing amnesia. There is a stopping place. Wrongs done between believers are judged and settled, and only when they are "cleansed and purified" is entry permitted. What Allah removes in ayah 47 is what remains once that judgment has already been passed. Mercy here does not bypass justice; in the order the hadith gives, it follows it.

**Which grudges does this mean?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises an obvious difficulty. There is a report it describes as appearing in Sahih Hadith — it names no collection — to the effect that "anyone who nurses the least grudge in his heart against a Muslim will not go to Jannah." If that is so, how do people arrive at the gates still carrying *ghill*?

The answer given is a careful distinction, and it is one of the most practically useful things in this passage:

1. **Chosen malice** — grudge "rooted in material ends, and is there by one's personal intention and choice, and because of which this person keeps looking for an opportunity to inflict pain or loss on his enemy." That is the blameworthy kind the warning addresses.
2. **Natural temperament** — "being ill at ease in someone's company as a matter of natural temperament, a human trait beyond one's control, is not included here."
3. **A grievance resting on some Islamic legal ground** — likewise not included.

It is this second and third kind, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, that our ayah promises to lift: "such grudge and temperamental distaste will be removed from their hearts." The point is a merciful one. You are not held to account for a chemistry you did not choose. You are held to account for what you *do* with it — for nursing it, feeding it, waiting for your chance.

**ʿAli's hope.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that it was about this kind of grudge that Sayyidna ʿAli said: "I hope that I shall be, along with Talha and Zubayr, among those the dust of mutual anxiety from whose hearts will be removed while entering Jannah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the reference: the difference of opinion and resulting conflict that took place between Sayyidna Talha, Sayyidna Zubayr and Sayyidna ʿAli.

Hold on to the image he chose — *dust*. Not a stain, not a verdict: dust, of the kind that is brushed off at a doorway. That is the tone in which a Muslim may hold his own quarrels, and the hope he may hold for them.

**"Brothers, facing each other on thrones."** The ayah does not stop at removal; it states the replacement. Brothers — and facing one another. Nobody at the back of the room, nobody looking at the back of a head. Ibn ʿAbbas's words, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits them, fill in the inner side of that same scene: "they all will feel love for each other in their hearts."

## Ayah 48 — No fatigue, and no eviction

"No sense of fatigue shall touch them, nor shall they be asked to leave it."

**"No sense of fatigue."** The Arabic word is *naṣab*. Ibn Kathir glosses it "meaning no harm or hardship," and cites, from the Sahihs, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah commanded me to tell Khadijah the good news of a jeweled palace in Paradise in which there will be no toil and no fatigue." The Arabic of that hadith closes on the same word our ayah uses — *naṣab* — so the glad tiding given privately to Khadijah is the promise held out here to every believer.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why this matters more than it first appears. In this world hard work naturally results in fatigue — but so does rest: "even a state of total rest and fun would sometimes tire a person out, no matter how enjoyable are things one is occupied with." Our capacity for enjoyment has a ceiling; we tire of pleasure itself. In Jannah that ceiling is gone.

**"Nor shall they be asked to leave it."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 48 as closing off, one by one, the ways a good thing can end:

1. *It runs out.* Answered in Surah Sad: "This is sustenance provided by Us which is never to exhaust" (38:54). The blessings of Jannah "shall never diminish."
2. *You are put out of it.* Answered by the words of our ayah: they "shall never be deprived of the state of bliss bestowed upon them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the contrast with worldly comfort — the recipient of the best of conveniences here lives under the apprehension that the owner of those facilities may become displeased with him one of these days and turn him out. That apprehension is exactly what ayah 46 already promised to remove; "security" is now shown to be a fact about the place, not merely a feeling in the guest.
3. *You grow bored of it and want out yourself.* This third possibility, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the Qur'an demolishes in one sentence of Surah Al-Kahf: "They will have no desire to be removed from it" (18:108) — a verse Ibn Kathir cites at the same point.

Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith at this ayah, without naming a collection for it, in which it will be said: "O dwellers of Paradise! You will be healthy and never fall sick; you will live and never die; you will be young and never grow old; you will stay here and never leave." Four announcements, and each one cancels a specific dread that shadows every good thing in this life.

## Ayat 49–50 — The announcement

Then the passage lifts out of description entirely and becomes a command: "Inform My servants ˹O Prophet˺ that I am truly the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. And that My torment is indeed the most painful torment." Ibn Kathir renders the command "Declare to My servants." Either way, the Prophet ﷺ is being told to carry a message, and the message is about who Allah is.

Ibn Kathir's paraphrase of the pair is direct: "O Muhammad, tell My servants that I am the source of mercy and I am the source of punishment." Both come from Him.

And Ibn Kathir tells us what the pairing is for. Verses like these, he says, "indicate that we must always be in a state between hope (for Allah's mercy) and fear (of His punishment)."

## Living it

Read together, the passage asks a few concrete things of a believer.

**Hold hope and fear together.** Ayah 49 alone breeds complacency; ayah 50 alone breeds despair. They were revealed as a pair and are meant to be carried as a pair. Ibn Kathir's phrase — *between* hope and fear — describes the healthy heart, and when you notice yourself drifting to one side, the other ayah is the correction.

**Take your grudges seriously, but not fatally.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's distinction gives you a test you can apply tonight: is this feeling something I am *choosing* to keep alive, watching for a chance to inflict pain or loss on someone — or is it a temperamental discomfort I did not ask for and cannot control? The first is the malice the warning addresses. The second is the dust Allah promises to brush off at the door of Jannah.

**Settle what you can settle here.** The report Ibn Kathir cites from the Sahih puts a bridge before the gate, where wrongs between believers are judged. Whatever you clear now — an apology made, a debt returned, a right restored — is business you will not be detained over there.

**Let the description do its work.** Peace with no problems, security with no fear of expulsion, hearts washed clean, brothers face to face, no fatigue, no ending, no boredom. Nearly every clause in ayat 45–48 answers something that spoils happiness in this life. That is the shape of what has been prepared for the people of Taqwa.
